1:
The title of the psalm is the first thing in dispute. Augustine of Hippo builds his exposition on it: it is inscribed a song of Jeremiah and Ezekiel on account of the people of the transmigration when they were beginning to go forth, and he rehearses the captivity, the prophecy of the seventy years, and the restoring of the temple. Adam Clarke rejects the same title outright. The Hebrew and the best copies give only a psalm and song of David; the ascription to the two prophets accords neither with the subject nor with the truth of history, since, as Calmet remarks, they were never found together before, at, or after the captivity — and he notes drily that one printed edition adds Haggai to the pair with equal propriety. John Calvin lists the conjectured occasions and refuses them all: Mudge’s traveller newly come to Jerusalem after deliverance from the fury of the sea, the thanksgiving for rain after the famine that followed the rebellion of Absalom, and Morrison’s feast of tabernacles. Keil and Delitzsch describe rather than date it: a congregation gathered round the sanctuary, rescued from an imperilled position among the nations and now at peace among fields rich in promise.

On the waiting of praise Charles Ellicott reports the literal words as to thee silence praise, which is hardly intelligible; the Greek and Latin read praise is comely, but he would supply a conjunction and render it quiet and praise — submissive expectation until the deliverance comes, and then exulting praise — adding that the next clause is better as, the vow is paid. Matthew Henry keeps the silence: praise is silent as wanting words for the goodness of God, and it waits as the Levites waited by night in the house of the Lord, ready to sing at the appointed hour. C.H. Spurgeon makes the same image a company of musicians gathered to welcome a prince, who wait till he appears. John Gill gives three reasons why praise waits in Zion: it is due there, the people bring it there, and it remains and continues there.

Charles Ellicott holds the promise that all flesh shall come to have been truly fulfilled in the calling of the Gentiles, but warns against letting that fulfilment hide what the poet consciously intended, since the psalm shows the exclusiveness of Hebrew belief along with the nobler feelings struggling against it: the privilege of praise belongs to Israel, while all flesh may approach in prayer. Adam Clarke takes it as the same prediction, then turns aside to warn preachers by an instance he witnessed, of an immensely corpulent minister who opened his address with these very words and laid a strong emphasis on all flesh.

The prevailing iniquities divide them again. Adam Clarke calls the received rendering no just translation: the words are that iniquitous words have prevailed against him, calumnies and slanders propagated to shake his confidence and ruin his credit; and he adds that the verse has been abused to favour Antinomian licentiousness, which the correct translation prevents. Charles Ellicott keeps the confession but makes it national: though the pronoun is singular we are to think of Israel confessing by the mouth of the poet, and he finds an antithesis between iniquity, the frailty common to all flesh, and transgression, the violation of the covenant. John Gill allows both readings and prefers his own indwelling sins, too mighty for him. On the man whom God chooses Adam Clarke thinks of the priests permitted to draw near, with the rest worshipping at the temple; John Gill of election in eternity and effectual calling in time; John Wesley of drawing near in the ordinances; and Charles Ellicott notes that both the relative and its antecedent are wanting, so that we should perhaps read, he whom thou choosest and bringest near shall dwell.
5:
What the terrible things are divides the entry at once. John Gill excludes afflictive dispensations on a procedural ground — afflictions are not prayed for and there is neither direction nor example for praying for them, so they cannot be reckoned answers of prayer — and makes them judgments on the enemies of God’s people, as at the Red Sea, in the wilderness and in the land of Canaan, and hereafter in the destruction of antichrist. Adam Clarke refers them instead to the wonderful displays of providence in the change of the seasons and the fertilising of the earth, and notes that the Latin joins the clause to the preceding verse. Charles Ellicott reads the word adverbially, wondrously, and the verb as a present describing the usual course of providence rather than the future of our version, the Greek and Latin turning it into a prayer instead. John Wesley refers the righteousness to God’s faithfulness and goodness. C.H. Spurgeon keeps the terror and turns it on the one who prays: we do not always know what we are asking for, and when the veritable answer comes it may terrify us — we seek sanctification and trial is the reply, we ask for more faith and more affliction is the result, we pray for the spread of the gospel and persecution scatters us.

On the confidence of all the ends of the earth Charles Ellicott declines to narrow the phrase to Israel in exile and gives the words their widest range, that consciously or unconsciously the whole world rests in God; Adam Clarke makes it the people scattered through the world and the isles of the sea, and reports that this too is understood of the vocation of the Gentiles. On the mountains Adam Clarke presses a single image: they were pitched into their places by the mighty hand of God and are preserved from splitting or mouldering as though by a girdle, hooped about by the divine power. Charles Ellicott sees the same girding as an Oriental workman’s, the divine Architect girt for his labours, and thinks the poet had in mind that empires no less than mountains owe their stability to God. Matthew Henry adds that though the mountains are called everlasting and are sometimes shaken by earthquakes, the covenant is said to stand more firmly than they.

Whether the stilled sea is literal or figurative is the second division. Charles Ellicott watches the literal pass into the figurative: from the raging seas the poet’s thought goes to the anarchies arising from the wild passions of men, for which the ocean has furnished metaphors in all literature, and he notes that Virgil reverses the simile, likening the sudden calm after the storm to the effect a leader of men produces in a seditious city. Adam Clarke keeps both together: God is sovereign over earthquakes, over the flux and reflux of the sea and over every tempest, and over the headstrong multitude too, for he stills the madness of the people. John Gill hears the stilling done by a word, as our Lord did it when here on earth, and takes it for a proof of his eternal power and Godhead. Matthew Henry says simply that God commands silence among the waves and lays them to sleep. On the tokens that frighten the uttermost parts John Gill canvasses the sun, moon and stars set for signs, or thunder and lightning, or the miracles wrought in the first times of the Gospel; John Wesley lists thunders, earthquakes, comets and strange meteors, and divides the verse between works extraordinary and terrible and works ordinary and delightful; and Adam Clarke, having listed tornadoes and eclipses among the same tokens, breaks off to declare that from this verse to the end of the psalm there is a series of the finest poetic imagery in the world.
9:
C.H. Spurgeon pictures the visit as a gardener’s round: the Lord surveys his garden and gives water to every plant that requires it, not in small quantities but until the earth is drenched, and he turns the verse into a prayer for his own parched and withering piety, quoting a verse that asks the graces to drop from above on a stock that lies dead. John Gill collects the visitations — the watering of the whole face of the ground before rain ever came upon it, the particular care of the land of Judea, and the general seasons of the whole earth — and applies them to the church, which is God’s husbandry and drinks in the rain that comes often upon it. Adam Clarke represents God as going through the whole globe, examining the wants of every part and directing the clouds where to deposit their showers and the rivers where to run.

What the river of God is divides them. Adam Clarke reports that some take it for the Jordan, with the visiting and watering referring to rain after a long drought, but suggests the clouds may be so called, being properly the origin of rivers. Charles Ellicott makes it simply the rain, and produces two proverbs: an Arabic saying that when the river of God comes the river at Bagdad ceases, and a rabbinic one that God has four keys which he never entrusts to any angel, chief of these the key of the rain. The word river, he adds, is very apt for the downpour of a country that has its rainy season, as in the phrase about the rushing of the river rain. John Wesley says the same in a line, that rain is called a river for its plenty and God’s for his immediate providing. C.H. Spurgeon notes that the brooks of earth are soon dried up and every human resource is finite, while this river has neither bottom nor shore.

On the ridges and the furrows Charles Ellicott would transpose the two English words, since what is rendered settling means literally pressing down, that is, the softening of the ridges of earth between the furrows; he notes that the Greek and Latin read multiply its shoots instead, that showers is literally multitudes of drops, and that our version misses the sense of the previous clause, which is that God prepares their corn when he has so prepared the land. Adam Clarke narrates the agricultural year instead: in seedtime the measure of rain necessary to prepare the earth for the plough, then, when the ridges are thrown into furrows, the showers that soften them for the expansion of the seed, and then the provident care that forms the ear and fills it, so that one grain yields thirty, sixty, a hundred or a thousand fold. John Gill follows Kimchi in taking the ridges for the eminences of ploughed land, which are brought low by the watering and made fruitful, and then reads them as men lifted up with their own imaginary righteousness, who when grace takes hold of them are humbled and confess themselves the chief of sinners. John Wesley keeps to the ground: the rain dissolves the high and hard clods of earth.
11:
The crowning of the year is a metaphor of encircling rather than of completion, Charles Ellicott argues: the Hebrew word, like the Greek, probably means to encompass, as when Lucretius has a wood crowning the waters, and the sense is that God made a year already prosperous still more abundant. Adam Clarke reaches the same word by another road — thou encirclest, as with a diadem — and calls it a most elegant expression for the progress of the sun through the twelve signs, producing the seasons and giving light and heat by turns to every part of the globe through its declination on each side of the equator; the very shape of that band on a celestial globe, he says, shows how properly the poet conceived the idea of a circle. John Gill takes the whole circling year and its harvest, and reads it further as the acceptable year of the Lord, in whose seasons there have been great gatherings of souls.

The paths that drop fatness are read as orbits by both the closest readers. Adam Clarke renders the word thy orbits and distributes the work among the planets revolving within the zodiacal space, or else among the twelve months of the solar revolution, since the rains of November and February and the frosts and snows of December and January are as necessary to the soil as the gentle showers of spring; the earth’s daily turning, its yearly circuit and the moon’s course are all wheels of God that produce fertility. Charles Ellicott notes that the root means to roll, and often the track made by a wheel, which suits the chariot of clouds God is elsewhere made to ride — though there with wrath, and here with plenty following in the track, as in the invocation where the winds flee and the earth sends up sweet flowers. He prefers, however, to take the word as revolutions and to think of the blessings brought by the seasons as they roll.

On the last two verses Adam Clarke explains that wilderness and desert in these writings generally mean places uninhabited and uncultivated rather than barren, and takes the girding of the hills with exultation from the frisking of lambs and the dancing of shepherds in the joy-inspiring summer. Charles Ellicott makes the sudden clothing of eastern hill-sides with plant life a fair mantle thrown round their shoulders, as if to deck them for a festival. John Wesley notes only that the wilderness, neglected by men, is furnished with food for beasts, and that the fields in their manner sing the praise of their benefactor. John Gill reports an alternative rendering in which the rams cover the flocks, and reads the clothed pastures as the multitude of converts gathering about the church. Adam Clarke closes with the whole scene at once — cattle in every plain and vista, valleys waving with harvest, and the cheerful songs of the peasantry, the singing of the birds, the neighing of the horse, the lowing of the ox and the bleating of the sheep, which he says are not unmeaning sounds but one great concert celebrating the bounty of God. He borrows from Claudian the green vesture of the mountains, and then declares the description inimitable and the nervous Hebrew not half expressed even by his own amended translation.
